method: Full read of all five independent automated publisher-audio transcriptions, aligned to canonical captions by matching utterance sequences and argument boundaries. No direct listening is claimed.

regions.finding: Horn frames a sincerity argument, concedes unequal martyrdom evidence and states willingness to suffer for the eleven, Paul and James; four deaths have stronger evidence. Paulogia appreciates the nuanced approach. Neither side claims all deaths are equally documented.

Paulogia initially says Alphaeus and promptly corrects to Zebedee. Horn quotes Acts 12, argues that brevity disfavors legendary embellishment, and grants the crucial question of why James was killed. Do not penalize the corrected name or garbled caption rendering of Herod.

Paulogia distinguishes political death from death establishing belief. Both grant harmonizable James traditions. Horn names Hegesippus, Clement and Josephus, invokes interwoven politics/religion and infers a religious charge from stoning; the inference remains argued, not externally verified.

Horn cites John 21, Second Timothy and Tacitus; the audio confirms hatred-of-mankind language and his move from fire scapegoating to religious persecution. Paulogia argues Nero might execute disliked leaders regardless of recantation, expressly concedes alternative scenarios are possible, and targets a guarantee while recognizing cumulative-case use.

Horn contrasts possibility and probability and cites Pliny/Trajan as judicial-process evidence. Paulogia challenges retrojection of a uniform policy and supplies Pilate as uneven-treatment evidence. Horn concedes no uniform Christian policy but argues broader Roman process and distinguishes extra-judicial misconduct. No external Roman-law verification is claimed.

Horn argues Christians could choose flight or continued danger before arrest. Paulogia asks whether easy recantation weakens willingness-to-die evidence. Horn answers with shame, lost standing, Donatist controversy and named apostates, connecting this with Clement’s endurance testimony. Automatic name spelling is not evidence of a speaker mistake.

Paulogia cites Peter’s restoration, clarifies his question concerns everyone beyond Peter and Paul, and argues life-saving defection may outweigh community costs. Horn distinguishes Jesus personally restoring Peter. Preserve the fact that the critic is disputing the inference, not affirming that all witnesses defected.

Horn uses Martin Luther King Jr and a hypothetical eleven associates to argue danger can support sincerity even without a formal recantation choice. Paulogia’s evidential challenge asks whether the apostles remained comparably associated; his photograph illustration concerns the modern comparison, not a demand for ancient photographs. He accepts Jesus had followers but limits confidence about later activity.

Horn explicitly separates sincerity from objective/veridical resurrection experience and distinguishes first-person experiences from inherited beliefs. Paulogia grants modern experiencers’ sincerity and questions Paul’s equivalence to pre-ascension bodily witnesses, using Moses/transfiguration as a possibility illustration. These are not denials of Paul’s sincerity.

The audio confirms Paulogia’s second-coming objection, Horn’s theophany response, and their explicit agreement that Paul sincerely believed he experienced Jesus. The trauma suggestion is expressly speculative; Paulogia distinguishes trauma from bereavement. Do not turn either explanation into a demonstrated psychiatric diagnosis or historical fact.

Horn develops Luke’s group-description analogy, Acts 4:33 and 5:40–42, and 1 Corinthians 15:11 as support for collective preaching. Paulogia grants that preaching is ordinary but disputes historical warrant and persistence beyond Acts 5; his skepticism concerns the evidence, not a proven departure of every unnamed apostle.

The audio confirms the Acts 8/14 correction, Epaphroditus, apostle as messenger, Horn’s distinction between preaching and eyewitness status, and the wedding-vow analogy for legitimate collective inference. Do not penalize garbled Greek, references or short mixed interjections; retain each side’s distinctions.

Paulogia tests the scope of “they” in 1 Corinthians 15 by the five hundred. Horn acknowledges a difference for formal preaching and points to apostle in verse 9; Paulogia explicitly accepts the correction. His later “everyone is very vague” claim is qualified by granting named preachers and distinguishing later church fathers from the New Testament.

Both acknowledge threats to church leadership and Paul’s persecution testimony. Horn invokes Paul’s Jerusalem contacts; Paulogia names Peter, James and John and asks how they establish the rest. The Dale Allison attribution is qualified: Paulogia admits he did not ask that exact continued-association question. Fishing and retained-name scenarios are proposed possibilities, not documented departures.

The caption gap is a mixed clarification about First/Second Timothy authorship: Paulogia doubts authorship by Paul or within his life; Horn says he had deliberately said “the author”; Paulogia acknowledges that. The surrounding exchange contests early organization, elders and Pauline networks. Missing caption words remain ineligible as an exact source span or independent rating basis; no uncorrected false attribution or silence inference may be drawn.

Horn’s conclusion stresses risk and some common ground before defending the wider group. His Sanders appeal explicitly concedes Sanders might not endorse all apostles. Paulogia grants sincere believers, presses evidence for all eleven, and describes a minimal-witness hallucination possibility. Do not portray the proposal as an established naturalistic reconstruction.

Horn replies to the concluding imprecision objection with collective Acts/Paul evidence and church networks, then favors comparing explanatory narratives. Both concluding arguments are present. Later invitations, thanks and channel promotion are outside scope. The audio and captions match the substantive end by utterance, without assuming a constant timestamp offset.

limitations: Both renderings are automatic, with isolated non-English substitutions and name errors in the secondary output; those cannot become exact quotes, factual corrections or score penalties.
Agreement of automatic outputs is evidence of content, not proof of historical claims or every literal syllable.
The caption-gap handoff is clarified but its missing words remain ineligible as selected caption evidence under the frozen source restriction.
